newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: FORECAST - Philippine trade gap may widen to $12 bln.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Philippine trade gap may widen to $12 bln.

text.p: The Philippines' eight-month trade deficit figure announced on Wednesday has led to expectations the gap for the full year would widen further to $12-12.5 billion, economists said.
"From a forecast of $11.5 billion, we've moved it up to $12.0 to $12.5 billion," Jose Mario Cuyegkeng, an economist of ING Barings Securities said.
The National Statistics Office on Wednesday reported the trade deficit for the January to August period widened to $8.147 billion versus $5.559 billion in the year-ago period.
"We were (earlier) looking at $10 billion for the whole year. The trade deficit would probably hit $12.0 billion," said Ernesto Pernia, a senior economist of Asian Development Bank.

The eight-month figures showed that import growth outpaced exports. Imports rose by 26 percent to $21.197 billion from $16.766 billion, while exports increased by 16 percent to $13.051 billion from $11.207 billion.
Despite the expectations of a wider trade deficit, economists say a drastic depreciation of the peso is not necessary.
Recently, some economists had said that the almost static movement of the peso for most of the year may have contributed to the wider trade deficit.

The peso hit a year-low of 26.28 to the dollar last Monday, a mere 0.3 percent weaker than the 26.20 at which it traded at the start of the year. By mid-session on Wednesday, the peso had recovered to 26.269 to the dollar.
"There is no major reason for the peso to weaken. The trade deficit should not be a big factor for a major depreciation," said Rolando Valenzuela, senior vice president of Philippine TA Securities.
Analysts said the wider trade deficit had been fueled mostly by capital equipment imports and a slowdown in electronics exports in line with the worldwide trend.
But the trade gap had been funded by term financing, direct and portfolio investments, as well as portfolio investments, they said.
They said the country's balance of payments position, lower inflation rate and the interest rate premium of the peso all combined to limit any slide in the peso.
"The market just expects it (the peso) to hover around 26.30 pesos," ING Baring's Cuyegkeng said.
But to contain the trade deficit, Pernia said "my preference is a slow depreciation rather than a sudden, drastic depreciation."
He said a rapid depreciation could be a "double-edge sword" because it could be favourable on the export side but would impact badly on inflation.
If the peso is allowed to weaken, "26.40 pesos is a worst case scenario for me. It can even be lower than 26.30 by year-end," said an economist, who declined to be identified.

He added that if the peso dips to 26.30 pesos, that would only be a 0.4 percentage point depreciation from the 26.20 at which the peso traded at the start of the year. The movement would be minimal when compared to the 6.0 percentage points premium the peso enjoys over the dollar.
